name: Donald Trump

summary.text: Donald Trump is a New York real-estate developer, casino operator and the 45th and 47th president of the United States; his business holdings are grouped under the Trump Organization. New Jersey casino regulators put his total debt at $3.4 billion in 1990, and his Atlantic City casino companies went through Chapter 11 reorganizations in 1991-92, 2004 and 2009. In September 2022 the New York Attorney General sued him, his adult sons and the Trump Organization under Executive Law 63(12), alleging his annual statements of financial condition inflated his net worth to obtain loans on better terms. Justice Arthur Engoron found the defendants liable and in February 2024 ordered about $355 million in disgorgement plus interest and a three-year bar on Trump serving as an officer or director of a New York company. On August 21, 2025 the Appellate Division, First Department, upheld liability and the injunctive relief but vacated the monetary award as an excessive fine.

facts.claim: In June 1990 Trump missed an interest payment on the Trump Castle casino's debt, and his lenders entered restructuring talks. The banks extended his deadlines and provided a $65 million loan, but set a $450,000-a-month personal allowance and required new managers, financial controls and asset sales. A New Jersey casino regulators' report in August 1990 put his total debt at $3.4 billion, including $1.3 billion on the casinos, of which $832.5 million was personally guaranteed by Trump.
facts.quote: The banks extended his deadlines and provided a $65 million loan, but they also set a $450,000-a-month personal allowance and required new managers, financial controls, and asset sales. A New Jersey regulators' August 1990 report put his total debt at $3.4 billion, including $1.3 billion on the casinos, and $832.5 million of which was personally guaranteed by Trump.

sources.title: The Atlantic City summer that nearly ruined Donald Trump

facts.claim: In December 1990, when the Trump Castle needed an $18.4 million interest payment, Fred Trump bought about $3.3 million in casino chips at the Castle, giving his son the cash to pay. The New Jersey Casino Control Commission investigated the purchase the next year and fined the Trump Castle $65,000, while allowing it to keep the cash.
facts.quote: Trump needed an $18.4 million interest payment, and his father bought about $3.3 million in casino chips at the Castle, which gave his son the cash to pay. The Casino Control Commission investigated the move the next year and fined the Trump Castle $65,000, but allowed it to keep the illegally obtained cash.

facts.claim: The Trump Taj Mahal entered a prepackaged Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 1991; the Trump Castle and Trump Plaza casinos in Atlantic City and the Plaza Hotel in New York followed with Chapter 11 filings in 1992. Trump used bankruptcy protection to restructure the debts of companies within the Trump Organization; later casino-company filings came in 2004, 2009 and 2014.
facts.quote: Trump agreed to a prepackaged Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 1991... He could not keep up with debts on two other Atlantic City casinos, and those two properties declared bankruptcy in 1992. Separately, the Plaza Hotel in New York declared bankruptcy in 1992 after amassing debt.

facts.claim: Trump Hotels & Casino Resorts filed for Chapter 11 in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Camden, New Jersey, in November 2004, after a proposed deal with Credit Suisse First Boston was rejected by bondholders. Under the preliminary agreement announced in October 2004, bondholders swapped some debt for equity and Trump's stake was to fall from about 47 percent to 27 percent. Trump described the filing as 'really just a technical thing.'
facts.quote: Under that plan, Donald Trump's stake would drop from about 47 percent to 27 percent. He said the filing was 'really just a technical thing'.

sources.title: Trump casinos file for bankruptcy
The Donald dumped in casino bankruptcy

facts.claim: Trump Entertainment Resorts, the successor company, filed for Chapter 11 again in February 2009 after bondholders, who had granted several waivers delaying an interest payment, threatened an involuntary bankruptcy. Trump resigned as chairman shortly before the filing, saying he disagreed with the bondholders' actions; his earlier offer to buy the company had been rejected. The reorganization that followed cut Trump's equity to 5 percent of the new stock plus warrants for another 5 percent, and Carl Icahn, who had bought debt from Andrew Beal, later gained control of the company.
facts.quote: Bondholders had granted several waivers to delay an interest payment, and they threatened to force the company into involuntary bankruptcy. Trump resigned as chairman of the board shortly before the filing, saying he disagreed with the bondholders' actions.

facts.claim: Deutsche Bank made its first loan to Trump in April 1998: $125 million to renovate 40 Wall Street, at a time when, according to journalists' accounts, several major banks had stopped lending to him after his companies' bankruptcies. In 2008, as repayment of a $640 million Deutsche Bank construction loan for the Trump International Hotel & Tower in Chicago came due, Trump sued the bank in New York State Supreme Court for $3 billion, invoking the financial crisis as a force majeure event; the bank countersued for the $40 million he had personally guaranteed. The dispute was settled on undisclosed terms.
facts.quote: He sues Deutsche Bank in New York State Supreme Court for $3 billion, claiming it's 'one of the banks primarily responsible for the economic dysfunction we are currently facing.' ... The bank sues Trump to at least get back the $40 million he personally guaranteed.

facts.claim: The New York Times reported on October 2, 2018 that Trump received the equivalent of at least $413 million from his father's real-estate empire, much of it through tax avoidance strategies in the 1990s, based on more than 100,000 pages of documents including confidential tax returns. Trump's lawyer Charles Harder called the allegations '100% false, and highly defamatory.' The same day a spokesman for the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance said the department 'is reviewing the allegations in the NYT article and is vigorously pursuing all appropriate avenues of investigation.'
facts.quote: A spokesman for the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance, James Gazzale, said the department 'is reviewing the allegations in the NYT article and is vigorously pursuing all appropriate avenues of investigation.'

sources.title: New York state tax department reviewing fraud allegations involving Trump in NYT article
Trump committed 'outright fraud' in 'dubious tax schemes,' according to a big, new investigation from The New York Times

facts.claim: On July 15, 2015, Trump's campaign announced that he had filed his personal financial disclosure with the Federal Election Commission. The campaign's release stated that his net worth was 'in excess of TEN BILLION DOLLARS,' reported 2014 income of $362 million, and said the form's categories top out at '$50 million or more.' The figure was the campaign's own characterization, not an audited valuation.
facts.quote: As of this date, Mr. Trump's net worth is in excess of TEN BILLION DOLLARS.

facts.claim: Trump's 2025 public financial disclosure, filed with the U.S. Office of Government Ethics on June 13, 2025 and covering 2024, reported $57,437,927 in income from token sales by World Liberty Financial and stated that he held 15.75 billion World Liberty governance tokens. The filing reported income of at least $217.7 million from Mar-a-Lago and his other Florida golf clubs.
facts.quote: The filing states the income as '$57,437,927,' detailing that the gain was realized through token sales. ... The filing reveals that Trump holds 15.75 billion governance tokens in World Liberty Financial.

facts.claim: Trump's annual financial disclosure released by the Office of Government Ethics on June 30, 2026, covering 2025, reported about $515 million from the sale of World Liberty Financial tokens and $65 million from sales of equity in the firm's holding company, with total crypto-related income reported at more than $580 million; Mar-a-Lago income was reported at roughly $77-80 million.
facts.quote: CNBC put the figure at about $515 million from the sale of tokens released by the firm World Liberty Financial, and $65 million from sales of equity in WLF's holding company.

facts.claim: On September 21, 2022, New York Attorney General Letitia James sued Trump, Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump, Eric Trump, the Trump Organization and others under Executive Law 63(12). The complaint alleged that Trump's annual statements of financial condition from 2011 through 2021 contained more than 200 false or misleading asset valuations that inflated his net worth by billions of dollars to obtain loans on more favorable terms, including statements submitted to Deutsche Bank as guarantor on a $125 million loan and a $170 million construction loan. The office sought disgorgement of about $250 million and bars on the defendants serving as officers or directors of New York companies.
facts.quote: Trump, with the help of his children and senior executives at the Trump Organization, allegedly inflated his net worth by billions of dollars to induce banks to lend money on more favorable terms. ... They were used to secure a $125 million loan from Deutsche Bank and were regularly submitted to the bank to fulfill the financial reporting requirements of Mr. Trump as guarantor on the loan.

sources.title: Attorney General James Sues Donald Trump for Years of Financial Fraud
Verified Complaint, People of the State of New York v. Donald J. Trump et al. (Supreme Court, New York County)

facts.claim: In November 2022 the trial court ordered the defendants to stop the alleged conduct pending trial and directed the appointment of an independent monitor over the Trump Organization (preliminary injunction order entered November 3, 2022).
facts.quote: The monitor originated in a Preliminary Injunction Order entered November 3, 2022, which directed the appointment of a monitor.

sources.title: Court Rules in Favor of Attorney General James and Orders Donald Trump and the Trump Organization to Immediately Stop Engaging in Financial Fraud

facts.claim: On February 16, 2024, Justice Arthur Engoron of the New York Supreme Court found Trump liable and ordered him to pay $354,868,768 in disgorgement, below the $370 million the Attorney General had requested, plus about $98.6 million in prejudgment interest accruing at 9 percent a year. The judgment barred Trump from serving as an officer or director of any New York corporation, and from applying for loans from New York-chartered banks, for three years; Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump were barred for two years and assessed about $4 million each, and former CFO Allen Weisselberg $1 million.
facts.quote: James had asked Engoron to ban Trump for life from New York's real estate industry, and for $370 million in disgorgement. Instead, Engoron fined Trump $354,868,768 in disgorgement. He also ordered Trump to pay a total of $98.6 million in prejudgment interest, which will accrue at an annual rate of 9%.

sources.title: New York judge orders Trump to pay more than $350 million in civil fraud suit
Decision and Order after Non-Jury Trial, People v. Trump (Sup. Ct. N.Y. County, Engoron, J.)
Attorney General James Wins Landmark Victory in Case Against Donald Trump

facts.claim: Engoron's decision found that the defendants had submitted false financial data to their accountants, producing fraudulent statements of financial condition that inflated Trump's assets by hundreds of millions to billions of dollars over several years, and rejected the defense that outside accountants were responsible for verifying the figures. He wrote: 'The frauds found here leap off the page and shock the conscience.' He also found that Weisselberg and Jeffrey McConney 'cannot be entrusted with controlling the finances of any business' and permanently barred them from financial-control roles at New York companies.
facts.quote: The frauds found here leap off the page and shock the conscience.

sources.title: QUOTES: Judge Engoron's Blistering Ruling Against Donald Trump
Judge imposes $364 million penalty in Trump's New York civil fraud case

facts.claim: In computing disgorgement, Engoron found that Deutsche Bank had set interest rates on its loans to Trump entities too low because of Trump's misstatements of his net worth in the personal guarantees, and, using the state's expert's figures, put the bank's interest shortfall across the projects at $168,040,167, of which about $126.8 million related to the loan for the Old Post Office hotel in Washington; he described his estimates as 'conservative.' The state's expert, Michiel McCarty, had compared the rates Trump obtained with personal guarantees against the rates proposed without them.
facts.quote: Using a figure from the state's expert, he put the bank's shortfall at $168,040,167 for the projects, and the judge described his estimates as 'conservative'.

facts.claim: In March 2024 the Appellate Division, First Department, reduced the bond the defendants had to post to appeal from the full judgment (about $464 million with interest) to $175 million, and stayed the officer-and-director and lending bans pending appeal. Trump posted the $175 million bond.
facts.quote: In March 2024, the New York Appellate Division, First Department, lowered the defendants' required bond from $464 million to $175 million, while staying the bans ordered by Engoron.

sources.title: Trump's massive civil fraud penalty for exaggerating financial statements is thrown out by appeals court
Appellate Division, First Department stay decision, People v. Trump

facts.claim: On August 21, 2025, a five-justice panel of the Appellate Division, First Department (People v Trump, 2025 NY Slip Op 04756), vacated the disgorgement award of about $464.6 million, holding it an excessive fine under the Eighth Amendment, while leaving in place the injunctive relief, including the temporary bars on Trump and his two eldest sons serving in corporate leadership in New York. The lead opinion by Justice Moulton, joined by Presiding Justice Renwick, stated that the trial court 'correctly found defendants liable' under Executive Law 63(12) and that 'the injunctive relief ordered by the court is well crafted to curb defendants' business culture.'
facts.quote: While the injunctive relief ordered by the court is well crafted to curb defendants' business culture, the court's disgorgement order, which directs that defendants pay nearly half a billion dollars to the state of New York, is an excessive fine that violates the Eighth Amendment of the United States Constitution.

facts.claim: The August 2025 appellate decision had no majority opinion on liability. Justices Higgitt and Rosado concurred in part and dissented in part in an opinion by Justice Higgitt that would have ordered a new trial limited to some transactions, and Justice Friedman wrote separately that he would have dismissed the complaint outright, concluding the Attorney General lacked authority to bring the case under Executive Law 63(12). Justices Higgitt and Rosado joined the decretal paragraph 'for the sole purpose of ensuring finality,' providing a path to appeal to the Court of Appeals. Attorney General James said she would seek review of the ruling on the penalty.
facts.quote: Because none of the three decisions garners a majority, Justices Higgitt and Rosado join the decretal of this decision for the sole purpose of ensuring finality, thereby affording the parties a path for appeal to the Court of Appeals.

openQuestions: The 1990 figures ($3.4 billion total debt, $832.5 million personally guaranteed, $450,000 monthly allowance, $65 million bank loan) come from CNN and Mother Jones summaries of the August 1990 New Jersey Casino Control Commission report; the commission's report itself was not reached. The Washington Post's Ferguson article on the Atlantic City casinos (reprinted in a House Judiciary hearing record at congress.gov) was returned in the search but not opened.

Bankruptcy details: sources differ on the Taj Mahal's debt at filing ($675 million vs. a missed $47.3 million bond payment) and on the Plaza Hotel's debt (one source says over $550 million; another says Trump gave up a 49% stake to lenders). Neither figure is recorded. Court dockets for the 1991-92, 2004 and 2009 cases were not opened.

The 1998 $125 million loan and the 2008 Chicago lawsuit are recorded from journalists' accounts (WNYC/ProPublica Trump, Inc.; FT via Irish Times; Net Interest); the court filings were not opened and the settlement date is given variously as 2010 and 2012. The site's '$300M' Deutsche Bank figure was not found; the complaint cites $125 million and $170 million loans and the Chicago loan was $640 million.

Engoron's decision PDF (ag.ny.gov trump-decision.pdf) and the First Department slip opinion (nycourts.gov 2025_04756) were returned by searches but their text was not read in full; the figures and quotations come from Courthouse News, U.S. News/Reuters, PBS/AP, NPR, Just Security, Forbes and New York Appellate Digest summaries. The $168,040,167 Deutsche Bank interest-shortfall figure and the $126.8 million Old Post Office share should be checked against the decision. Whether the monitor and compliance director were explicitly addressed in the August 2025 decision was not confirmed.
Whether the Attorney General filed for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeals, and any ruling there, was not researched.

The 2015 disclosure is recorded from the campaign's press release (American Presidency Project copy); the FEC/OGE form itself was not opened. The 2025 and 2026 OGE filings were not opened; figures are from Cointelegraph, Forbes, Fortune, CNBC and CBS reports. Outlets round the 2024 World Liberty figure differently ($57.4M vs $57.7M).
The 2018 New York Times tax investigation could not be opened; it is recorded via CNBC's same-day summaries. The state tax department's investigation outcome was not found.

The search tool returned some summaries without a per-sentence attribution; quotes in this file were checked against the result text but the owner should confirm them on the cited pages, in particular the Just Security passage on the $168 million figure.
